title: Detect unauthorized or suspicious Hardware Additions (USB/Thunderbolt/Network)
shortTitle: Detect unauthorized or suspicious Hardware Additions (USB...
summary: This strategy detects hardware additions that bypass normal procurement and endpoint controls, such as unauthorized removable storage, a rogue network adapter, or a Thunderbolt or PCI device plugged into a running workstation. The technique matters because physical access converts a hardened endpoint into an attacker controlled one: a device can present itself as a keyboard, capture keystrokes, or provide a bridging network path that skips perimeter controls entirely. Detection rests on device installation telemetry from the endpoint, driver and service installation records that fire when new hardware is recognised, process creation from driver installation paths, and the inventory of hardware already approved for that asset. It fails in practice because docking stations, badge readers, headsets and presentation adapters are plugged in constantly, so the rule needs a per asset baseline of permitted device classes rather than a blanket alert on new hardware.

beginner.definition: This detection looks for new hardware attached to a computer, mainly small devices plugged into a port. Examples are memory sticks, mobile broadband adapters and external network cards. It compares the new device against what the computer is allowed to have. Anything unexpected is reported for review.
beginner.whyItMatters: Someone who can touch a computer can often do things remote controls cannot stop. A small device can record every key press or open a second network path. Some devices are also used to steal data quickly. Physical access is common in shared offices, labs and reception areas.
howItWorks: The system records the moment a new device is recognised and its driver is prepared.
It records the driver or service installation that follows the new device.
It records which account and process were active at that moment.
The asset inventory supplies the list of device classes allowed on that machine.
A SIEM (Security Information and Event Management system) compares each event to that list.
A device class outside the list, or one paired with an unusual driver, raises the alert.
beginner.example: Think of a staff entrance with a visitor book. Visitors sign in and wear a badge, which everyone expects. A person who walks straight to the server room without signing in is the one the receptionist remembers.
takeaways: Physical access can defeat many controls that work well over the network.
The useful baseline is the device classes each asset is allowed to see.
Alert value comes from pairing the new device with unusual driver or process activity.

objectives: Explain how a newly attached device can capture input or create a network path.
Identify which telemetry records device recognition and driver installation on an endpoint.
Build a per asset baseline of permitted device classes and approved hardware identifiers.
Correlate a device installation with the account and process active at that time.
Decide which physical locations and asset groups justify strict hardware alerting.
dataSources: Windows Security event 6416 device recognition, which records when an external device is first seen by the system
Windows Security event 4697 service installation recorded when a new driver backed service is registered on the host
Sysmon event 6 driver load events showing the loaded driver image and its signature status
Windows Security event 4688 process creation with command line auditing enabled, showing the process that ran during device installation
Endpoint device control or data loss prevention logs listing removable media connections with the device identifier and policy outcome
logic: The detection is a comparison, not a single event. It takes every device installation on a host, extracts the device class and vendor or product identifiers, and compares them with the set of devices that host is expected to support. It then enriches the finding with the driver installed, the signature status of that driver, and the account or process active when the device appeared. Fields that must line up are the host, the device identifier, the driver image path, and the time of installation. The benign case repeats across many hosts: the same model of docking station, keyboard or approved encrypted storage that already appears in the fleet inventory, installed by the system itself with a signed driver. The malicious case is a device class that never appears elsewhere in the estate, on a host in a publicly reachable area, installing an unsigned driver from a temporary path, often followed by bulk file access or a short lived second network interface.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Unapproved Hardware Device Installed With Unsigned Driver
# logsource:
#   product: windows
#   category: driver_load
# detection:
#   selection:
#     EventID: 6
#     SignatureStatus: 'Unavailable'
#   filter_approved:
#     Image|contains:
#       - '\\SystemRoot\\System32\\drivers\\disk.sys'
#       - '\\SystemRoot\\System32\\drivers\\usbhub.sys'
#   condition: selection and not filter_approved
# level: medium
falsePositives: IT provisioning technicians who attach approved encrypted storage devices to new laptops during a hardware rollout
Shared meeting rooms where users plug in presentation adapters, webcams and conference microphones that are not in the asset inventory
Reception and warehouse staff connecting barcode scanners, signature pads or label printers supplied by a partner
Support engineers using a vendor diagnostic dongle that presents as an unrecognised serial device on the host
tuningNotes: Collect the device class and hardware identifier for every installation for a month, then build an allow list per site and per asset group so that a common adapter is expected where it belongs but not in the server room. Escalate automatically for hosts in publicly accessible areas, for devices that present as input devices on a machine that already has a keyboard, and for drivers that fail signature verification, while leaving ordinary storage on well managed laptops at a lower severity. The coverage you lose by allowing common storage device classes is data theft using an approved looking device, so retain a rule that alerts on unusually large file reads or writes coinciding with removable media connection.
